title: Slipstream SLO relaxation and regional circuit escort
author: Maya Patel
description: Context: Several customers running multi-region deployments observed spiky SLO breaches during short-lived regional network storms. The existing regional circuit breaker aggressively tripped and tenant-level SLO quotas caused cascading evictions when a region briefly underperformed. Motivation: Reduce user-visible errors while keeping global capacity protections intact. This PR introduces a two-part mechanism: 1) Slipstream SLO relaxation: transient, time-windowed softening of tenant SLO enforcement based on short-term regional health signals (slipstream windows). 2) Circuit Escort: an escorting path that keeps a minimal number of warm requests routed through a secondary region while the primary circuit transitions, preventing rapid cold-start thrashing and losing all in-flight KV cache benefit. Design summary: - Slipstream windows: when regional upstream health indicates >=2x baseline tail latency or increased error rate, tenants with recent successful requests get a short-lived SLO relaxation token (configurable TTL, default 15s) that increases their eviction threshold by a fractional budget (default +10%). Tokens are per-tenant-per-region and decay linearly. - Circuit Escort: when a regional circuit moves from healthy->degraded or degraded->open, select N escort slots per tenant (configurable; default 2) to route shadowed requests to an adjacent healthy region with warm KV hinting and priority lane so they do not contend with cold traffic. Escorted requests are rate-limited and excluded from standard eviction accounting; they are used to keep per-tenant KV slices warm during transient regional disruptions. Implementation notes: - Runtime: added slipstream token generator in region-monitor service. Tokens are signed ephemeral keys stored in Redis with TTL and a histogram eviction key for decay. - Router: enhanced route decision to consult slipstream token and escort table; added escort path that sets X-Escort: true and attaches KV-hint header. - Policy: new SLOPolicy flags and fallbacks; default conservative values kept; feature gated behind runtime flag "slipstream_enabled" for staged rollout. - Observability: new metrics: slipstream.tokens_issued, slipstream.token_hit_ratio, escort.active_slots, escort.kv_hint_success_rate; added dashboard panels and SLO regression alert. Testing & QA: - Unit tests cover token lifecycle, decode/validation in router, and escort flow selection. - Integration: local multi-region integration harness (benchmark-lab) simulated 30s region latency spikes and validated that the slipstream window reduced tenant-level evictions by ~78% in the experiment and overall error budget burn by ~62%. - Load test: perf-canary run with 2k concurrent tenants showed escort slots did not increase p95 server CPU. Rollout plan: 1) Canary enable on a small set of internal tenants for 48 hours. 2) Gradual ramp on non-production regions for 72 hours. 3) Controlled exposure to customers with a feature flag opt-in. Rollback: runtime flag and gate allow immediate disable; Redis token TTLs ensure full revert within TTL window (default 15s) after disable. Risk and mitigation: - Risk: misconfiguration could allow a noisy tenant to consume extra capacity; mitigated with per-tenant caps and cross-tenant usage metrics + alerting. - Risk: escort path could add tail latency if the secondary region is not actually healthy; mitigated by health checks and KV-hint success gating before escorting. Related work: follows ENG-1928 (regional failover playbook) and builds on router changes from ENG-1973. Notes: This is intentionally conservative — token amounts and escort slots are small by default to avoid changing global behavior until we validate telemetry in canary.

review_comments: Ethan Chen: Can we make the default token TTL configurable per-tenant? Concerned about long-lived tokens during prolonged incidents.
